chunks: "PCB rework is any process where you take an already-assembled board and remove, replace or modify something on it.
Usually that means desoldering a part and soldering a new one in, but it also covers adding jumper wires, cutting traces, or fixing a bad solder joint.
The reasons are things like a manufacturing defect, say a bridge or a tombstoned resistor, a component that failed or was the wrong value, or a design change after the boards were already built.
I'd also separate rework from repair: rework brings the board back to its original spec, while modification changes the design and repair restores damaged copper or laminate.
The important thing is that it's a controlled process, not just touching it with an iron.
You need the right temperature profile for the alloy, flux, a way to preheat the board so you're not shocking it, and ESD protection.

Every cycle puts extra heat into the board and can lift pads or damage nearby parts, which is why standards like IPC-7711 and IPC-7721 limit what's allowed and why a shop will often scrap a cheap board instead of reworking it.
And as a designer I try to make rework easy: good spacing, no hidden parts under big BGAs, and test and bodge options on the board."
